opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. One of the nice things about regular languages is that they give you a setting where you actually know what the right answer looks like. With natural language, when a model does something impressive, it's very hard to say what computation is underneath. With a family of regular languages, especially when you generate a fresh automaton per example and ask the model to learn it in context, you know exactly what an ideal learner should be doing. So you can ask a sharper question: not just "does it get the answer right," but "what algorithm is it implementing?"

What surprised me, and changed how I think about these models, is that the answer often wasn't the elegant one you'd write down as a computer scientist. You might expect a transformer learning a new regular language in context to infer something like the underlying state machine. What we tended to find was closer to a statistical shortcut. The model was computing something like in-context n-gram statistics: looking back over the prompt for places where the same recent context occurred and using what came next to predict the next token. That turned out to be a large part of what separated architectures that did well from those that struggled. Transformers seemed to find these "n-gram head" circuits fairly easily, and some recurrent and state-space models did less well on this kind of task, even though in principle they're a natural fit for regular languages.

That had two consequences for me. First, it made me more cautious about reading too much into a model's behavior. A model can look like it's doing structured, symbolic inference when it's actually doing smart counting, and those come apart once you push on the distribution. Second, it was constructive. Once we understood the mechanism, we could add that kind of n-gram computation as an explicit inductive bias to other architectures, and that helped not only on the synthetic tasks but somewhat on real language modeling. So the synthetic setting wasn't only diagnostic. It told us something about what a good language model needs to be able to do.

More broadly, it pushed me toward a view I hold pretty strongly now. "What computation does this network perform?" is answerable, but only if you choose problems where you already understand the space of possible solutions. Formal languages are one of the best tools we have for that. They let you treat interpretability less like reading tea leaves and more like hypothesis testing.

r001.rationale: The response says the models often used in-context n-gram statistics rather than inferring the underlying state machine.

r002.rationale: It describes the surprising computation and its research implications, but does not suggest that weaker initial assumptions would have accelerated the project.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it made me a lot more humble about the stories I'd been telling myself about what these models "know."

When you train a sequence model on data generated by a finite-state machine, you have this wonderful situation where the ground truth is completely legible. You know exactly what the minimal automaton looks like, you know what the states are, you know what the transitions are. So the question becomes very sharp: does the network recover that structure, or something else?

And what you find is a mixed picture. Sometimes the hidden states really do cluster in a way that lines up with the automaton's states, and you can read off something that looks like the right transition function. But very often the model finds a representation that's sufficient for prediction without being isomorphic to the generating machine. It'll merge states that happen to be indistinguishable under the training distribution, or it'll split a state into several because of some incidental feature of the data, or it'll solve the problem with a kind of counting mechanism when the "textbook" solution involves no counting at all.

That reframed how I think about interpretability more generally. There's a temptation to assume that if a model gets the right answers, it must have found the same abstraction a human would write down. The regular-language experiments were a clean demonstration that this isn't guaranteed even in the simplest possible setting. The model is optimizing for prediction under a particular distribution, and there are typically many internal procedures that achieve that. Which one you get depends on architecture, on initialization, on the specific way the data is sampled.

The other thing it taught me is that you have to be careful about your evaluation. If you only test on strings from the training distribution, a model with a "wrong" internal mechanism can look perfect. It's only when you probe with inputs that distinguish the hypotheses, longer strings, unusual paths through the automaton, that the differences surface. That's pushed a lot of my later work toward asking not just whether a model succeeds, but what it would take to tell apart the different ways it could be succeeding.

So I'd say the main shift was from thinking of interpretation as discovering the algorithm the model learned, to thinking of it as a hypothesis-testing problem where you have to actively design inputs that can falsify your favorite story about the computation.

r001.rationale: The response says models may learn several non-isomorphic mechanisms, including counting, but never identifies their computation as essentially n-gram prediction.

r002.rationale: The response describes becoming more humble about assumptions, but does not suggest that weaker initial assumptions could have accelerated the research project.

astra-6.text:
One thing it changed was how willing I was to infer a model’s internal computation from the task it was solving. With regular languages, you have a very clean account of how you could solve the problem: build a finite-state machine, track its state as you read the sequence, and use that state to decide what can come next. So it’s tempting to assume that a neural sequence model trained on that data will discover something like that machine.

But matching the behavior of a finite-state machine doesn’t mean you’ve learned the same algorithm. A model might exploit patterns that work on the lengths and examples it sees during training, without learning a computation that continues to work on longer sequences. And even when it does generalize, its representation needn’t look like the symbolic description we started with.

So I came away thinking of these simple languages as a useful laboratory. You know what information is sufficient to solve the task, and you can ask whether the network preserves that information, how it represents it, and where the computation breaks down. That makes the distinction between learning to predict well and learning a particular computational procedure much more concrete.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the models learn a finite-state machine, but it does not identify their computation as essentially n-gram prediction.

r002.rationale: The response discusses being cautious about inferring a model’s computation, but does not suggest that weaker initial assumptions could have accelerated the research project.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me much more cautious about inferring what a model has learned from its accuracy. With a regular language, you have a very clean description of the computation that would solve the task: there’s a finite-state machine, and you can ask whether the network’s hidden states actually correspond to the states of that machine.

And the interesting thing is that getting the predictions right doesn’t necessarily mean learning that computation. A model can exploit patterns that work on the lengths or examples it sees during training, but behave differently when you push it outside that distribution. Even when it does learn a good solution, its internal representation needn’t look like the compact symbolic description we started with.

So those experiments gave me a way to separate two questions that we often conflate: can a network produce the right answers, and what procedure is it using to produce them? Regular languages are a useful setting because you can make that second question unusually precise.

r001.rationale: The response says models may exploit training-set patterns and that their representations need not match a finite-state description, but it does not identify their learned computation as essentially n-gram prediction.
